text: Selection sort works by continuously selecting the minimum from the unsorted section of the array, and then placing it in the sorted section of the array, using a swap. Suppose the input to the algorithm is array A indexed from 1 to n. The pseudo-code is given below: for i= 1 to n-1 min_index = i for j = i+l ton if A[j] < Almin_index] min_index = j Swap A[min_index] and A[i] 1 ... ....BBBBBBBBnBBBBBBBBBBBBBB . Each iteration of the the inner for loop runs in constant time, say d. There are n — 1 iterations of the inner for-loop when i = 1, accounting for a total time of d(n — 1). There are n — 2 iterations of the inner for-loop when i = 2, accounting for a total time of d(n — 2). The pattern continues and the sum of all the operations carried out by the inner for loop is exactly: =1 dn—1)+dn—2)+...+d(1) =d<%) There are also exactly n — 1 swaps that are performed, and each swap takes constant time, say k, accounting for k(n — 1) time. The total runtime is therefore d (@) + k(n —1). We can show this is O(n?): -1 T(n)=d (%) +k(n—1) <dn?/2+kn < dn® + kn? = (d + k)n® Note that in the above analysis, the number of steps performed is always the same, regardless of the input. Therefore the best-case and worst-case runtimes are identical: they are both O(n?). This differs from Insertion Sort, which has a best-case runtime of O(n). Therefore if there is a high chance that your input is sorted, Insertion sort should be preferred.
